subject: Boat survey design for flying birds

messages.author: e479aa417c59f1ba
messages.subject: Boat survey design for flying birds
parts:
Hello

=20

I am designing a boat survey to estimate tern densities. Our survey area
will approximately be a coastal strip c. 40km long out to 20km offshore,
which encompasses the breeding colony. As all birds will be flying, we
are using a snapshot count method (essentially point counts) with
distance bands within a 180 degree arc ahead of the boat, out to 300m.

=20

I would like some advice on the best way to get a systematic random
design for the point counts for such a boat survey. I was planning to
use the Distance programme to design zig-zag line transects within our
survey area. I was then going to have the point count positions located
at e.g. 1km intervals along the transect. The idea is that the boat will
travel at speed between count points, but slow down to allow the count
to be made instantaneously.

=20

First question is how do I ensure that the point counts are allocated
randomly (but systematic)? Could I randomly assign the first count point
within the first 1km of the transect, and then space them at equal
distance from that one?

=20

Secondly, there will be areas of lower density further offshore, so I
would like to have less effort (fewer point counts) in this area (to
reduce survey time). Can I simply space the point counts e.g. every 2km
instead of 1km in this area, if so how do I then deal with this reduced
effort during analysis stages? Or do I first need to split the survey
area into two strata, design the zig-zag transects, and then position
the point counts.=20

=20

Or should I be doing something completely different?!

=20

Thanks

Linda

=20

=20

Linda J Wilson

Senior Seabird Ecologist

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Boat survey design for flying birds
parts:
Linda:

I can appreciate that you'd like your boat to travel in a zigzag for
efficiency, and that you want to do snapshots at regular intervals.
However, if you place your snapshots at fixed distances along the
transects, they probably won't end up being systematic with respect to
each other (because of the zigzag). Is it impractical to use the
Distance survey design engine (systematic grid sampling) to place a set
of systematic points into your study area, then after that design is
created, connect up the pattern of points in the most efficient manner?

Your second matter about differing amounts of effort at distances
offshore could most simply be addressed by the stratification mechanism
you describe. I believe the Mexico sample project that comes with
Distance is an example of placing differing amounts of sampling
intensity within different strata.

That's my view, but other design mavens may have more clever ideas.
